latin.title: Horace's Monument More Lasting Than Bronze
latin.body: In 23 BCE, Quintus Horatius Flaccus completed his first three books of Odes with a bold declaration: his poetry would outlast the pyramids and survive until the final priest climbed the Capitoline. The son of a freedman who fought on the losing side at Philippi, Horace had rebuilt his life through patronage and verse. His claim to immortality was not hubris but calculation. Bronze corrodes, marble cracks, empires fall, but poems live in memory and on papyrus. He had watched Augustus transform Rome with monuments of travertine and marble, yet Horace knew that syllables arranged in Sapphic and Alcaic meters could prove more durable than any stone. The first line of that final ode became a commonplace among later poets: exegi monumentum. Two millennia later, students still parse his hexameters while most Augustan architecture lies in fragments.

greek.title: Oedipus Learns His True Name
greek.body: In Sophocles' Oedipus Tyrannos, first performed around 429 BCE, the moment of anagnorisis arrives not through a token or scar but through the convergence of testimonies. A messenger from Corinth announces Polybus' death, intending comfort: Oedipus need not fear killing his father. But his news unravels everything. The messenger reveals he once received an infant on Mount Cithaeron, ankles pierced. The Theban shepherd confirms he gave that baby away to save it from exposure. Jocasta flees the stage in silence, understanding first. Oedipus follows the logic to its end, demanding the shepherd speak. The recognition completes itself in mathematics: one infant, one mountain, one set of scars. Aristotle praised this structure because the discovery emerges from the plot itself, not from contrivance. The hero's name, meaning 'swollen foot,' had carried the truth all along.

french.title: Racine's Phèdre at the Hôtel de Bourgogne
french.body: On January 1, 1677, Jean Racine's Phèdre premiered at the Hôtel de Bourgogne before Louis XIV's court. The actress Marie Champmeslé, Racine's collaborator and rumored lover, created the title role with such intensity that witnesses reported she trembled visibly as Phèdre confessed her illicit desire. Racine adapted Euripides and Seneca, but his heroine speaks in the formal alexandrines of French classical tragedy, bound by the strict unities of time, place, and action. The play sparked immediate controversy: a rival troupe staged Pradon's competing Phèdre et Hippolyte the same week, backed by Racine's enemies at court. Yet Racine's version endured. His Phèdre becomes a woman destroyed not by divine curse alone but by her own consciousness of guilt, trapped between passion and moral law in twelve-syllable couplets of devastating precision.

german.title: Schiller's Astrological General at Pilsen
german.body: In February 1634, Albrecht von Wallenstein summoned the astrologer Giovanni Battista Seni to his headquarters at Pilsen. The general, commander of the imperial armies, refused to march without consulting the stars. Seni calculated planetary positions, cast horoscopes, advised on auspicious days. Wallenstein delayed, negotiated secretly with Sweden, and was assassinated by his own officers on February 25. Friedrich Schiller seized on this historical entanglement of military power and celestial determinism for his trilogy. In 'Wallensteins Tod' (1799), the general faces a web of political intrigue while clinging to Seni's predictions. His tragedy lies not in blind fate but in his attempt to read it, to force history into alignment with Jupiter and Saturn. Schiller found in this seventeenth-century condottiere a perfect subject for exploring how belief in Schicksal becomes self-fulfilling prophecy.

oldenglish.title: Kennings in the Beowulf Manuscript
oldenglish.body: The Beowulf poet never wrote 'body' when he could say bānhūs, bāncofa, or flǣschoma—bone-house, bone-chamber, flesh-garment. These kennings, compound metaphors unique to Germanic verse, allowed the scop to vary his half-lines while maintaining alliterative meter. A ship became a mere-hengest (sea-steed), the sea a hwælweg (whale-road), blood swāt (sword-sweat). The technique served both practical and aesthetic ends: it solved metrical problems while satisfying an audience trained to decode poetic riddles. By the time a Benedictine scribe copied Beowulf into Cotton Vitellius A.xv around the year 1000, this older oral tradition was already fading. The manuscript preserves nearly 1200 of these archaic compounds, many found nowhere else in surviving Old English. When fire swept Sir Robert Cotton's library in 1731, the vellum edges charred and crumbled, taking unknown kennings with them into ash.
